_comment: French sentence-level constructions whose meaning is not recoverable word-by-word.
Gap steps may forbid tokens with '!': *<=5!pas|plus keeps restrictive ne...que from
firing on a plain negation followed by a complementizer que.
This is the hand-seeded core; the curated inventory extends it.

constructions.schema_form: il n'y a pas que X
constructions.meaning_en: X is not the only thing — there is more to it than X.
constructions.why_opaque: Word-by-word this reads 'there is not that X', which sounds like a denial that X exists. It means the opposite: X does exist, it just isn't the whole story.
constructions.literal_trap: there isn't any X
constructions.example_fr: Il n'y a pas que l'argent qui compte.
constructions.example_en: Money isn't the only thing that matters.

constructions.meaning_en: Restricts to whatever follows 'que': only, nothing but.
constructions.why_opaque: 'ne' normally signals negation and 'que' normally means 'that', so the pair looks like a negated clause. Together they mean 'only' — a restriction, not a negation.
constructions.literal_trap: a negation plus 'that'
constructions.example_fr: Je n'ai que dix euros.
constructions.example_en: I only have ten euros.

constructions.meaning_en: Denies the restriction: not only X, but other things too.
constructions.why_opaque: It negates the ne...que restriction, so adding 'pas' turns 'only X' into 'not only X' — the opposite of what adding a negative word usually does.
constructions.literal_trap: does not have X at all
constructions.example_fr: Elle ne parle pas que du travail.
constructions.example_en: She doesn't only talk about work.

constructions.meaning_en: Adds a second, often stronger element to the first.
constructions.why_opaque: The two halves sit far apart, so a learner reading linearly finishes the first clause before realising a paired 'mais' is coming.
constructions.example_fr: Non seulement il est venu, mais il a aidé.
constructions.example_en: Not only did he come, he helped.

constructions.meaning_en: Two things increasing together.
constructions.why_opaque: French has no equivalent of English 'the' here, so the correlation is carried purely by repeating 'plus'. A learner reads the second 'plus' as a separate comparison.
constructions.literal_trap: more ... more
constructions.example_fr: Plus on attend, plus c'est difficile.
constructions.example_en: The longer you wait, the harder it gets.

constructions.meaning_en: Two things decreasing together.
constructions.why_opaque: Same missing 'the' as plus...plus — the correlation lives in the repetition alone.
constructions.literal_trap: less ... less
constructions.example_fr: Moins je dors, moins je me concentre.
constructions.example_en: The less I sleep, the less I concentrate.

constructions.meaning_en: Puts the spotlight on whatever sits between 'c'est' and 'que'.
constructions.why_opaque: Word-by-word it becomes 'it is X that ...', which sounds clumsy in English. French uses it routinely just to stress X, where English would use word order or intonation.
constructions.literal_trap: it is X that ...
constructions.example_fr: C'est demain que ça commence.
constructions.example_en: It starts tomorrow.

constructions.meaning_en: However much one does the action, it makes no difference.
constructions.why_opaque: 'beau' means beautiful, and nothing in the words carries concession or futility. It means roughly 'no matter how much', which is unguessable from 'to have beautiful'.
constructions.literal_trap: to have a beautiful ...
constructions.example_fr: Il a beau insister, je ne changerai pas d'avis.
constructions.example_en: However much he insists, I won't change my mind.

constructions.meaning_en: The action finished a moment ago.
constructions.why_opaque: Word-by-word it is 'to come from doing', suggesting movement or origin. It is actually a tense — the immediate past — with no English equivalent beyond 'to have just'.
constructions.literal_trap: to come from doing
constructions.example_fr: Je viens de finir.
constructions.example_en: I've just finished.

constructions.name_en: to be in the middle of doing
constructions.meaning_en: The action is in progress right now.
constructions.why_opaque: 'train' means train, and 'en train de' looks like a phrase of place or manner. It is French's way of marking the progressive, which the language has no tense for.
constructions.literal_trap: to be in the train of
constructions.example_fr: Elle est en train de lire.
constructions.example_en: She's reading right now.

constructions.name_en: causative faire (have or make something done)
constructions.meaning_en: Causing someone else to do the action, or having it done.
constructions.why_opaque: Reads as 'to do to do'. The subject does not perform the second verb — someone else does — and nothing in the words signals that.
constructions.literal_trap: to do X oneself
constructions.example_fr: J'ai fait réparer la voiture.
constructions.example_en: I had the car repaired.

constructions.name_en: it is a matter of / it's about
constructions.meaning_en: Introduces what the topic or issue actually is.
constructions.why_opaque: Impersonal and subjectless: 'il' refers to nothing, and 'agir' normally means to act. A learner looks for who is acting and finds nobody.
constructions.literal_trap: he acts about
constructions.example_fr: Il s'agit d'une erreur.
constructions.example_en: It's a mistake.

constructions.meaning_en: Accepting a cost or risk in order to do something.
constructions.why_opaque: 'quitte' looks like the verb 'to leave'. Nothing in the words conveys 'even at the cost of', which is what it means.
constructions.literal_trap: leaves to
constructions.example_fr: J'y vais, quitte à arriver en retard.
constructions.example_en: I'm going, even if it means arriving late.

constructions.meaning_en: Rejects both alternatives.
constructions.why_opaque: 'ne' carries the negation while 'ni' does the coordinating, so unlike English there is no single 'neither' word to latch onto.
constructions.example_fr: Il ne boit ni café ni thé.
constructions.example_en: He drinks neither coffee nor tea.

constructions.meaning_en: Gives the reason for the situation in the first clause.
constructions.why_opaque: 'si' sets up a condition, so a learner expects a consequence. Instead an explanation follows — the clause order reverses the logic English would use.
constructions.literal_trap: if ..., it is that ...
constructions.example_fr: S'il est parti, c'est qu'il était fatigué.
constructions.example_en: If he left, it's because he was tired.

constructions.meaning_en: Intensifies a quality and gives the reason for the intensification.
constructions.why_opaque: Four common words that together mean 'all the more so given that'. No individual word carries the causal link.
constructions.literal_trap: as much more that
constructions.example_fr: C'est d'autant plus surprenant qu'il avait promis.
constructions.example_en: It's all the more surprising given that he'd promised.

constructions.name_en: il n'y a que X (only X)
constructions.meaning_en: X is the only one / the only thing; X alone.
constructions.why_opaque: The existential frame plus ne...que gives an exclusive-identification meaning ('X and nobody else'), which no single word supplies.
constructions.literal_trap: 'There is nothing that X' — the negation is misattributed to the existence of X instead of to everything other than X.
constructions.example_fr: Il n'y a que toi qui puisses l'aider.
constructions.example_en: You're the only one who can help him.

constructions.meaning_en: hardly, scarcely, not much — a weakened, understated negation.
constructions.why_opaque: 'guère' has no independent meaning a learner can look up usefully; the pair means 'barely', which is neither full negation nor affirmation.
constructions.literal_trap: Treating it as a plain 'not', losing the understatement, or guessing it means 'not at all' (too strong).
constructions.example_fr: Ça ne m'étonne guère.
constructions.example_en: That hardly surprises me.

constructions.meaning_en: no X at all, not a single X — again with no 'pas'.
constructions.why_opaque: 'aucun' alone is a bare quantifier; the negative force comes from the ne...aucun frame, and 'pas' is banned inside it.
constructions.literal_trap: Adding 'pas', or reading 'aucun' as 'any' and so getting 'he didn't make any effort?' as a question or a positive 'some'.
constructions.example_fr: Il n'a fait aucun effort.
constructions.example_en: He made no effort whatsoever.

constructions.meaning_en: just / merely / the mere fact of — minimising: even this small thing is enough.
constructions.why_opaque: 'rien' means 'nothing' and 'que' 'that', yet together they mean 'just', a positive minimiser rather than a negation.
constructions.literal_trap: 'nothing that I think about it' — the negative 'rien' is read literally and the sentence collapses.
constructions.example_fr: Rien que d'y penser, j'ai froid.
constructions.example_en: Just thinking about it makes me cold.

constructions.meaning_en: unless — states the one condition that would cancel the main clause.
constructions.why_opaque: 'at less that' gives no clue; and the 'ne' that often follows is expletive, carrying no negation at all.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading the expletive 'ne' as a real negative: 'unless it doesn't rain' instead of 'unless it rains'.
constructions.example_fr: Nous partirons demain, à moins qu'il ne pleuve.
constructions.example_en: We'll leave tomorrow, unless it rains.

constructions.name_en: à moins de + inf (unless one does)
constructions.meaning_en: unless you/one does X — same exception meaning, with a shared subject and an infinitive.
constructions.why_opaque: 'at less of doing' is meaningless literally; the exceptive meaning is purely constructional.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading 'moins' as a quantity ('less than leaving now'), producing a comparative that is not there.
constructions.example_fr: À moins de partir maintenant, tu vas rater ton train.
constructions.example_en: Unless you leave now, you'll miss your train.

constructions.meaning_en: except X, other than X, if not X — an exceptive after a negative or a superlative.
constructions.why_opaque: It looks like a conditional clause 'if it is not', but it functions as the preposition 'except'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'if it is not him' — parsed as a real if-clause, which leaves the sentence with no coherent condition.
constructions.example_fr: Personne ne le sait, si ce n'est lui.
constructions.example_en: Nobody knows, except him.

constructions.name_en: ne serait-ce que (if only, even just)
constructions.meaning_en: if only, even just, if nothing else — concedes a minimal version of something.
constructions.why_opaque: A frozen conditional-with-inversion whose parts ('would it not be that') give no access to the concessive 'even just'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'wouldn't it be that five minutes' — read as a question or a negation instead of a minimising concession.
constructions.example_fr: Passe me voir, ne serait-ce que cinq minutes.
constructions.example_en: Come and see me, if only for five minutes.

constructions.meaning_en: to be well aware / to be by no means without — a double negative used as strong affirmation.
constructions.why_opaque: Two negatives ('not' + 'without') cancel into a polite emphatic positive, a rhetorical effect invisible in the words.
constructions.literal_trap: 'You are not without knowing' read as 'you don't know', i.e. the exact opposite of 'you are surely aware'.
constructions.example_fr: Vous n'êtes pas sans savoir que la situation est grave.
constructions.example_en: You are of course aware that the situation is serious.

constructions.meaning_en: without X happening — negates the subordinate event while keeping a positive main clause.
constructions.why_opaque: French packs the negation into the connector, where English uses a gerund; and an expletive 'ne' may appear inside without adding negation.
constructions.literal_trap: Adding a second negation in the subordinate clause, or reading the expletive 'ne' as real: 'without me not noticing'.
constructions.example_fr: Il est parti sans que je m'en aperçoive.
constructions.example_en: He left without my noticing.

constructions.schema_form: ce n'est pas que + subjunctive/indicative, ... mais ...
constructions.name_en: ce n'est pas que (it's not that)
constructions.meaning_en: it's not that X (I'm not denying X is imaginable) — pre-empts a wrong inference before giving the real reason.
constructions.why_opaque: A cleft frame used metalinguistically: it negates a possible explanation rather than a fact, and typically takes the subjunctive.
constructions.literal_trap: 'It is not that I don't want' read as a flat statement about wanting, losing the 'that's not the reason' function.
constructions.example_fr: Ce n'est pas que je ne veuille pas, mais je n'ai pas le temps.
constructions.example_en: It's not that I don't want to — I just don't have the time.

constructions.meaning_en: still, all the same, the fact remains that — concedes the previous point but maintains one's own.
constructions.why_opaque: Literally 'it doesn't prevent that', but it works as a one-word concessive adverb like 'still'; the negation is not about prevention at all.
constructions.literal_trap: 'It doesn't prevent that he is right' — learners hunt for what is being prevented and lose the discourse function.
constructions.example_fr: N'empêche qu'il a raison.
constructions.example_en: Still, he's right.

constructions.schema_form: il n'en reste pas moins que ...
constructions.name_en: il n'en reste pas moins que (the fact remains)
constructions.meaning_en: the fact nevertheless remains that X — concedes the preceding argument while insisting on X.
constructions.why_opaque: A frozen chain of negation, pronoun 'en' and 'moins' whose parts ('there remains of it not less that') decode to nothing usable.
constructions.literal_trap: 'There remains no less of it than...' — treated as a quantity statement rather than a concessive connector.
constructions.example_fr: Il n'en reste pas moins que le problème persiste.
constructions.example_en: The fact remains that the problem persists.

constructions.meaning_en: and neither does X / any more than X does — extends a negation to a second element.
constructions.why_opaque: Surface-identical to the comparative 'more than', but with 'pas' adjacent it becomes a negative additive, not a comparison of degree.
constructions.literal_trap: 'not more than you' read as a quantity comparison ('I knew less than you') instead of 'you didn't know either'.
constructions.example_fr: Je ne le savais pas, pas plus que toi.
constructions.example_en: I didn't know — and neither did you.

constructions.name_en: rien de moins que (nothing short of)
constructions.meaning_en: nothing short of X, no less than X — a strong emphatic upgrade.
constructions.why_opaque: A negation plus a comparative that together produce emphasis rather than a smaller quantity.
constructions.literal_trap: 'nothing less than a scandal' read as downplaying ('it's less than a scandal') rather than intensifying.
constructions.example_fr: C'est rien de moins qu'un scandale.
constructions.example_en: It's nothing short of a scandal.

constructions.schema_form: (il n'y a) rien de tel que X
constructions.name_en: rien de tel que (there's nothing like)
constructions.meaning_en: there's nothing like X — a superlative recommendation of X.
constructions.why_opaque: A negative existential used to praise: 'nothing of such kind as X' means X is the best.
constructions.literal_trap: 'nothing like a good coffee' read as 'this is not like a good coffee', i.e. as criticism of X.
constructions.example_fr: Rien de tel qu'un bon café le matin.
constructions.example_en: There's nothing like a good coffee in the morning.

constructions.schema_form: loin s'en faut / tant s'en faut
constructions.meaning_en: far from it, nothing like it — appended to reinforce a preceding negation.
constructions.why_opaque: An impersonal frozen expression built on 'falloir'; none of the four words points to 'far from it'.
constructions.literal_trap: Trying to parse 'it is needed of it so much' and abandoning the sentence, or reading it as 'almost'.
constructions.example_fr: Ce n'est pas terminé, loin s'en faut.
constructions.example_en: It's not finished — far from it.

constructions.name_en: n'avoir que faire de (to have no use for)
constructions.meaning_en: to have no use for X, to not care about X — dismissive.
constructions.why_opaque: 'to have only to do of X' has no compositional route to 'I couldn't care less about X'; 'faire' is frozen and 'que' is not restrictive in the usual way.
constructions.literal_trap: 'I only have to do with your advice', i.e. read as an obligation instead of a rejection.
constructions.example_fr: Je n'ai que faire de vos conseils.
constructions.example_en: I have no use for your advice.

constructions.name_en: on ne peut plus + adj (couldn't be more)
constructions.meaning_en: extremely, as X as can be — a superlative intensifier of the adjective.
constructions.why_opaque: An impersonal clause embedded as a modifier: 'one cannot more' has become a pure intensifier with no clausal meaning left.
constructions.literal_trap: 'one can no longer clear' — the learner tries to read 'on ne peut plus' as its own clause and the sentence breaks.
constructions.example_fr: Son explication était on ne peut plus claire.
constructions.example_en: His explanation could not have been clearer.

constructions.meaning_en: the more X, the less Y — inverse correlation.
constructions.why_opaque: The inverse-proportion reading exists only in the paired quantifiers at clause heads.
constructions.literal_trap: 'More I know him, less I like him' parsed as two unconnected clauses, or confused with 'plus ou moins' (more or less).
constructions.example_fr: Plus je le connais, moins je l'apprécie.
constructions.example_en: The more I get to know him, the less I like him.

constructions.meaning_en: the less X, the more Y — inverse correlation, other direction.
constructions.why_opaque: As above: the construction, not the words, encodes proportionality.
constructions.literal_trap: Treating the second 'plus' as 'no longer' (ne...plus) and negating the second clause.
constructions.example_fr: Moins il travaille, plus il se plaint.
constructions.example_en: The less he works, the more he complains.

constructions.name_en: d'autant moins que (all the less so because)
constructions.meaning_en: all the less X because — the stated reason reduces the degree.
constructions.why_opaque: Mirror of d'autant plus que, with the same non-compositional degree-plus-cause packaging.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading it as a plain comparative 'less ... than', which reverses the causal link.
constructions.example_fr: Il est d'autant moins excusable qu'il savait tout.
constructions.example_en: He is all the less excusable given that he knew everything.

constructions.meaning_en: especially since, all the more so as — adds a reinforcing reason.
constructions.why_opaque: 'of as much that' gives nothing; used alone (without plus/moins) it is a causal connector.
constructions.literal_trap: Expecting a comparison because of 'autant', and looking for the second term that never comes.
constructions.example_fr: Je n'irai pas, d'autant que je suis fatigué.
constructions.example_en: I won't go, especially since I'm tired.

constructions.name_en: autant ... autant ... (as much as ..., by contrast)
constructions.meaning_en: as much as X is true, so Y is true (in contrast) — sets two clauses in symmetric opposition.
constructions.why_opaque: The contrastive-symmetry meaning comes only from the doubled 'autant'; there is no 'but' or 'whereas' anywhere.
constructions.literal_trap: 'As much I love summer, as much I hate winter' — read as a comparison of amounts rather than a contrast.
constructions.example_fr: Autant j'aime l'été, autant je déteste l'hiver.
constructions.example_en: Much as I love summer, I hate winter.

constructions.meaning_en: as long as / while / so long as — temporal-conditional limit.
constructions.why_opaque: 'so much that' is the natural reading of the words, but adjacent 'tant que' means 'as long as' — a completely different relation.
constructions.literal_trap: 'So much that there is life' — confusing it with the consequence construction tant ... que.
constructions.example_fr: Tant qu'il y a de la vie, il y a de l'espoir.
constructions.example_en: Where there's life, there's hope.

constructions.meaning_en: so much / so many X that Y — degree leading to a consequence.
constructions.why_opaque: Split across the clause, 'tant' and 'que' form a degree-result frame; 'que' is neither 'that' as a complementiser nor 'than'.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading 'que' as 'than' and expecting a comparison, or confusing it with adjacent 'tant que' (as long as).
constructions.example_fr: Il a tant insisté que j'ai fini par céder.
constructions.example_en: He insisted so much that I eventually gave in.

constructions.meaning_en: so much / so X that Y — degree with consequence.
constructions.why_opaque: Same discontinuous degree-result frame; the consequence reading depends on both anchors being present.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading 'que' as 'than' ('he shouted so much than...') or as a relative pronoun.
constructions.example_fr: Il a tellement crié qu'il n'a plus de voix.
constructions.example_en: He shouted so much that he's lost his voice.

constructions.name_en: si bien que (with the result that)
constructions.meaning_en: so that, with the result that — introduces an actual consequence.
constructions.why_opaque: 'so well that' suggests quality; in fact it is a neutral result connector with no evaluation of 'well' at all.
constructions.literal_trap: 'so well that he arrived late' — the learner reads praise into 'bien' and the clause contradicts itself.
constructions.example_fr: Il a raté son train, si bien qu'il est arrivé en retard.
constructions.example_en: He missed his train, so he arrived late.

constructions.schema_form: de plus en plus (+ adj / de + N)
constructions.name_en: de plus en plus (more and more)
constructions.meaning_en: increasingly, more and more — a progressive increase over time.
constructions.why_opaque: 'from more in more' is meaningless; the dynamic 'increasingly' sense is carried by the whole frozen frame.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading it as a comparative 'more than' and looking for a second term.
constructions.example_fr: Il fait de plus en plus chaud.
constructions.example_en: It's getting hotter and hotter.

constructions.schema_form: de moins en moins (+ adj / de + N)
constructions.name_en: de moins en moins (less and less)
constructions.meaning_en: increasingly less, fewer and fewer.
constructions.why_opaque: Same frozen progressive frame as de plus en plus, unrecoverable from 'from less in less'.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading a static comparative ('less than') instead of a change over time.
constructions.example_fr: Il y a de moins en moins de monde.
constructions.example_en: There are fewer and fewer people.

constructions.name_en: pas mal de (quite a lot of)
constructions.meaning_en: quite a lot of, a fair number of — a positive, fairly large quantity.
constructions.why_opaque: 'not badly of' encodes quantity, not quality; the negation contributes nothing negative.
constructions.literal_trap: 'not bad' read as an evaluation ('the people are not bad') instead of as a quantifier.
constructions.example_fr: Il y avait pas mal de monde au concert.
constructions.example_en: There were quite a few people at the concert.

constructions.schema_form: il y a X qui + verb
constructions.meaning_en: X is ...ing — introduces a new subject as news; equivalent to a plain English sentence.
constructions.why_opaque: The existential 'there is' plus a relative clause is French's way of saying 'the phone is ringing'; the existential meaning is not really present.
constructions.literal_trap: 'There is the telephone which is ringing' — read as an existential claim about a phone existing.
constructions.example_fr: Il y a le téléphone qui sonne.
constructions.example_en: The phone's ringing.

constructions.meaning_en: and then, all of a sudden — marks an unexpected turn of events.
constructions.why_opaque: 'voilà' is normally a presentative 'here is'; immediately followed by 'que' it becomes a narrative surprise marker.
constructions.literal_trap: 'here is that it started to rain' — read as pointing something out rather than as 'and then suddenly'.
constructions.example_fr: On partait, et voilà qu'il a commencé à pleuvoir.
constructions.example_en: We were leaving, and then it started to rain.

constructions.meaning_en: I/we have been ...ing for X (and still am) — duration up to the present.
constructions.why_opaque: French uses a presentative plus the present tense where English needs a present perfect continuous; 'here is three hours that' decodes to nothing.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Here is three hours that I wait for you' — the tense and the duration relation are both lost.
constructions.example_fr: Voilà trois heures que je t'attends.
constructions.example_en: I've been waiting for you for three hours.

constructions.meaning_en: it has been X (amount of time) that / since — ongoing duration.
constructions.why_opaque: 'that makes' plus a time span is an impersonal duration frame; the present-tense verb after 'que' maps to an English perfect.
constructions.literal_trap: 'That makes two years that I live here' — read as a causal or arithmetical statement.
constructions.example_fr: Ça fait deux ans que je vis ici.
constructions.example_en: I've been living here for two years.

constructions.schema_form: il y a + duration + que + clause
constructions.meaning_en: it has been X amount of time that / since — duration, formal counterpart of 'ça fait ... que'.
constructions.why_opaque: The existential 'il y a' is recycled as a duration marker, and the following clause keeps a French tense that English renders as a perfect.
constructions.literal_trap: 'There is a long time that I have not seen him' — read as existential, and the negated passé composé is mistranslated as a completed past.
constructions.example_fr: Il y a longtemps que je ne l'ai pas vu.
constructions.example_en: I haven't seen him for a long time.

constructions.meaning_en: scarcely had X happened when Y happened — immediate succession.
constructions.why_opaque: 'hardly' plus 'that' produces a temporal 'no sooner ... than'; formal French also inverts the subject, which further hides the structure.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading 'que' as 'than' in a comparison, or as a complementiser, and losing the 'the moment X happened' timing.
constructions.example_fr: À peine était-il sorti que le téléphone a sonné.
constructions.example_en: No sooner had he left than the phone rang.

constructions.meaning_en: far from doing/being X — an emphatic denial of X.
constructions.why_opaque: A spatial word ('far') is used as a negator of degree; 'far from being stupid' is a full negation dressed as a distance.
constructions.literal_trap: Reading spatial distance, or hedging it to 'not very' instead of the strong 'anything but'.
constructions.example_fr: Il est loin d'être bête.
constructions.example_en: He's anything but stupid.

constructions.meaning_en: to be going to do something / to be about to do it
constructions.why_opaque: 'aller' loses its motion meaning entirely and becomes a pure future auxiliary, with no 'to' linking the two verbs; the same string can also still be literal motion, so the learner must choose.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Je vais lui parler' read as 'I go to speak to him' (physically going somewhere)
constructions.example_fr: Je vais lui parler ce soir.
constructions.example_en: I'm going to talk to him tonight.

constructions.schema_form: être + sur le point de + INFINITIF
constructions.name_en: imminence être sur le point de
constructions.meaning_en: to be on the verge of doing something
constructions.why_opaque: A spatial noun phrase ('on the point of') is recycled as a pure aspect marker for imminence; nothing in the words signals time.
constructions.literal_trap: 'sur le point de fermer' read as 'on the subject of closing' or 'at the closing point'
constructions.example_fr: L'entreprise était sur le point de fermer.
constructions.example_en: The company was on the verge of closing down.

constructions.meaning_en: to end up doing something, after a while or after resistance
constructions.why_opaque: 'par' does not mean 'by (means of)' here; the pair encodes 'eventually, in the end', which is a temporal notion absent from both words.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il a fini par accepter' read as 'He finished by accepting', i.e. accepting was the last thing he did
constructions.example_fr: Il a fini par accepter notre proposition.
constructions.example_en: He eventually accepted our proposal.

constructions.meaning_en: to do X as the first step (before other things)
constructions.why_opaque: It contrasts minimally with 'commencer à + infinitif' (to start doing), yet means something different: sequence, not onset. 'par' again is not instrumental.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Commence par lire la consigne' read as 'Start by reading' in the sense of 'begin reading' (= commencer à lire)
constructions.example_fr: Commence par lire la consigne, tu répondras après.
constructions.example_en: Read the instructions first, then answer.

constructions.meaning_en: to keep on doing something non-stop (usually annoyingly)
constructions.why_opaque: A negated verb yields a positive, intensified statement about frequency: the negation applies to the stopping, so the whole thing means 'does it constantly'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il n'arrête pas de se plaindre' read as 'He doesn't stop to complain'
constructions.example_fr: Il n'arrête pas de se plaindre du bruit.
constructions.example_en: He's constantly complaining about the noise.

constructions.meaning_en: to have almost done something (and not done it)
constructions.why_opaque: An affirmative past tense denies that the event happened: the event is asserted as nearly-but-not-actual, and 'faillir' is a verb learners never meet outside this frame.
constructions.literal_trap: 'J'ai failli tomber' read as 'I failed to fall' or 'I fell short of falling'
constructions.example_fr: J'ai failli tomber dans l'escalier.
constructions.example_en: I almost fell on the stairs.

constructions.meaning_en: to be supposed to do something (with a hint that it may not be happening)
constructions.why_opaque: 'censé' is a bound past participle with no independent use; the construction carries an implicature of non-compliance that no word states.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Tu es censé porter un casque' read as 'You are censored/deemed sensible to wear a helmet' (also confused with 'sensé' = sensible)
constructions.example_fr: Tu es censé porter un casque sur le chantier.
constructions.example_en: You're supposed to wear a helmet on the site.

constructions.name_en: ne pas manquer de (be sure to)
constructions.meaning_en: to be sure to do something / to do it without fail
constructions.why_opaque: A negated verb of lacking yields a strong positive commitment or a guarantee; the meaning ('definitely will') is the opposite of the surface 'not lacking'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Je ne manquerai pas de vous informer' read as 'I will not lack to inform you' / 'I won't miss informing you'
constructions.example_fr: Je ne manquerai pas de vous tenir informé.
constructions.example_en: I'll be sure to keep you posted.

constructions.schema_form: ne + avoir + qu'à + INFINITIF (aussi: il n'y a qu'à)
constructions.name_en: n'avoir qu'à (all you have to do is)
constructions.meaning_en: all that is needed is to do X / you just have to X
constructions.why_opaque: The restrictive ne...que attaches to a following infinitive and turns 'have' into 'the only required step is', frequently with an impatient or dismissive tone the words never show.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Tu n'as qu'à demander' read as 'You have only at to ask' or as a reproach 'you only ask'
constructions.example_fr: Si tu as besoin d'aide, tu n'as qu'à demander.
constructions.example_en: If you need help, all you have to do is ask.

constructions.schema_form: il + PRONOM (me / te / lui / nous / vous / leur) + faut
constructions.meaning_en: I / you / he ... need something
constructions.why_opaque: The needer is an indirect object, not the subject, and the subject 'il' refers to nothing; there is no verb 'to need' visible anywhere.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il me faut deux jours' read as 'He needs me two days' or 'it is necessary to me two days'
constructions.example_fr: Il me faut deux jours de plus pour finir.
constructions.example_en: I need two more days to finish.

constructions.name_en: impersonal obligation il faut que + subjunctive
constructions.meaning_en: someone must / has to do something
constructions.why_opaque: Personal obligation is expressed by an impersonal frame with a dummy 'il', and the real subject appears inside a subordinate clause that must be subjunctive; the obligation is on that subject, not on 'il'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il faut que tu partes' read as 'It is needed that you leave' with no sense of who is obliged, or produced with the indicative ('que tu pars')
constructions.example_fr: Il faut que tu partes maintenant.
constructions.example_en: You have to leave now.

constructions.schema_form: il s'agit de + NOM / INFINITIF (il ne s'agit pas de ...)
constructions.meaning_en: it is about X / what is at issue is X; (with an infinitive) what is required is to X
constructions.why_opaque: A reflexive of 'agir' (to act) used impersonally means 'be a matter of'; there is no acting, no agent, and the construction can never take a real subject (never 'ce livre s'agit de').
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il s'agit d'un malentendu' read as 'He acts of a misunderstanding' or 'he is dealing with a misunderstanding'
constructions.example_fr: Il ne s'agit pas de discuter, il s'agit d'obéir.
constructions.example_en: This isn't about arguing, it's about doing as you're told.

constructions.schema_form: il suffit de + INFINITIF / NOM (+ pour ...)
constructions.name_en: il suffit de (all it takes is)
constructions.meaning_en: all you need to do is X / X is enough (to cause the result)
constructions.why_opaque: An impersonal 'it suffices' with a dummy subject encodes minimal sufficiency, and the optional 'pour' clause supplies the consequence; often the pragmatic force is 'that's all it takes for things to go wrong'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il suffit d'appuyer' read as 'He is sufficient to press'
constructions.example_fr: Il suffit d'appuyer sur ce bouton pour tout annuler.
constructions.example_en: All you have to do is press this button to cancel everything.

constructions.schema_form: il suffit que + SUBJONCTIF (+ pour que + SUBJONCTIF)
constructions.meaning_en: it only takes X happening (for the consequence to follow)
constructions.why_opaque: Two subjunctive clauses chain a minimal cause to an outsized effect; nothing in the words expresses 'only', and English needs a completely different frame ('the slightest ... and ...').
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il suffit qu'il pleuve' read as 'it suffices that it rains' with no sense of 'the slightest rain and...'
constructions.example_fr: Il suffit qu'il pleuve pour que tout soit annulé.
constructions.example_en: The slightest bit of rain and the whole thing gets cancelled.

constructions.meaning_en: to make someone do something, or to have something done (by someone else)
constructions.why_opaque: Two verbs share one clause with no linking word, and the doer of the second verb becomes an object of 'faire' — so the subject of the sentence is precisely the person who does NOT perform the action.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Je fais réparer ma voiture' read as 'I repair my car' or 'I make repair my car'
constructions.example_fr: Je fais réparer ma voiture demain.
constructions.example_en: I'm getting my car repaired tomorrow.

constructions.meaning_en: to get X-ed (to have something done to oneself, often unpleasantly)
constructions.why_opaque: The reflexive marks the subject as the victim or beneficiary, not the agent: the subject undergoes the infinitive's action. It reads as an active sentence but means a passive one.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il s'est fait voler son vélo' read as 'He stole his own bike' or 'he made himself steal a bike'
constructions.example_fr: Il s'est fait voler son vélo devant la gare.
constructions.example_en: He had his bike stolen outside the station.

constructions.meaning_en: to let someone do something / to let something happen
constructions.why_opaque: Like the causative, two verbs share one clause with no 'to', and the permitted doer surfaces as an object; 'laisser' loses its 'leave behind' sense.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Laisse-moi faire' read as 'Leave me to do' / 'abandon me doing' instead of 'let me handle it'
constructions.example_fr: Laisse-moi faire, je m'en occupe.
constructions.example_en: Let me handle it, I'll take care of it.

constructions.meaning_en: to let oneself be X-ed, to put up with it without resisting
constructions.why_opaque: The subject is the undergoer and the construction adds a strong notion of passivity or failure to resist; 'ne te laisse pas faire' has no word for 'stand up for yourself', which is exactly what it means.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Ne te laisse pas faire' read as 'Don't let yourself do' or 'don't leave yourself to be made'
constructions.example_fr: Ne te laisse pas faire, réponds-lui !
constructions.example_en: Don't let them walk all over you, answer back!

constructions.meaning_en: as a result of doing something over and over / through sheer repetition
constructions.why_opaque: 'force' does not mean strength or coercion here: the phrase encodes repeated effort over time as the cause of a result, an aspectual notion no single word carries.
constructions.literal_trap: 'À force de répéter' read as 'by force of repeating', i.e. forcibly
constructions.example_fr: À force de répéter, il a fini par comprendre.
constructions.example_en: After going over it again and again, he finally got it.

constructions.meaning_en: however much / no matter how much someone does X, it makes no difference
constructions.why_opaque: 'beau' is frozen and invariable, has no article, and means nothing like 'beautiful'; the construction is the main clause yet functions as a concession, and the crucial 'but it changes nothing' is only implied by the following clause.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il a beau essayer' read as 'He has a nice try' or 'he had a good go at trying'
constructions.example_fr: Il a beau s'excuser, personne ne le croit.
constructions.example_en: He can apologise all he likes, nobody believes him.

constructions.meaning_en: even if it means X / at the risk of X
constructions.why_opaque: 'quitte' is a frozen invariable adjective here, unrelated to the verb 'quitter'; the phrase expresses an accepted cost or risk, which neither word states.
constructions.literal_trap: 'quitte à me fâcher avec lui' read as 'leaving to get angry with him'
constructions.example_fr: Je dirai la vérité, quitte à me fâcher avec lui.
constructions.example_en: I'll tell the truth, even if it means falling out with him.

constructions.meaning_en: even if / even though (hypothetically)
constructions.why_opaque: Three high-frequency words ('when', 'well', 'even') combine into a concessive conjunction with no temporal meaning at all, and it uniquely takes the conditional rather than the subjunctive.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Quand bien même il s'excuserait' read as 'when even well he would apologise'
constructions.example_fr: Quand bien même il s'excuserait, je ne lui pardonnerais pas.
constructions.example_en: Even if he did apologise, I wouldn't forgive him.

constructions.meaning_en: while at the same time doing X / even though one does X
constructions.why_opaque: 'tout' is not a quantifier here but a marker that turns the gerund concessive or strictly simultaneous; the frequent 'although' reading is completely invisible in the words.
constructions.literal_trap: 'tout en reconnaissant que j'avais raison' read as 'all in recognising that I was right'
constructions.example_fr: Il a refusé, tout en reconnaissant que j'avais raison.
constructions.example_en: He refused, while admitting that I was right.

constructions.meaning_en: whatever (someone does / says), no matter what
constructions.why_opaque: Two separate words meaning 'what' and 'that' produce a free-choice concessive; it is also one letter away from 'quoique' (although), so the split spelling is the only clue to which meaning is intended.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Quoi que tu fasses' read as 'What that you do' or as 'although you do'
constructions.example_fr: Quoi que tu fasses, préviens-moi avant.
constructions.example_en: Whatever you do, let me know beforehand.

constructions.schema_form: quel(le)(s) que + être au SUBJONCTIF + NOM
constructions.meaning_en: whatever / whichever X may be, regardless of X
constructions.why_opaque: An interrogative adjective plus 'que' plus a subjunctive 'être' yields a concessive; the adjective agrees with a noun that follows the verb, which no word-by-word reading predicts.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Quel que soit le résultat' read as 'Which that be the result'
constructions.example_fr: Quel que soit le résultat, on continuera.
constructions.example_en: Whatever the outcome, we'll carry on.

constructions.schema_form: aussi / quelque / tout + ADJECTIF + que + SUBJONCTIF
constructions.meaning_en: however X (someone or something) may be
constructions.why_opaque: The same words otherwise form a plain comparison ('aussi grand que moi'); only the subjunctive and the absence of a second term of comparison signal the concessive 'however X'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Aussi surprenant que cela puisse paraître' read as 'as surprising as that can appear' (a comparison)
constructions.example_fr: Aussi surprenant que cela puisse paraître, il a accepté.
constructions.example_en: Surprising as it may seem, he agreed.

constructions.name_en: purpose pour que / afin que + subjunctive
constructions.meaning_en: so that / in order that (someone else does something)
constructions.why_opaque: 'pour' means 'for' with a noun and 'in order to' with an infinitive, but with 'que' it opens a full clause that must be subjunctive; the switch is triggered purely by whether the subject changes.
constructions.literal_trap: 'pour que tu sois prêt' read as 'for that you are ready', or produced with the indicative 'pour que tu es prêt'
constructions.example_fr: Je te le dis maintenant pour que tu sois prêt.
constructions.example_en: I'm telling you now so that you'll be ready.

constructions.meaning_en: so as to, in such a way as to
constructions.why_opaque: A noun of manner plus 'à' expresses intended result; the contrast with 'de manière à ce que + subjonctif' (different subject) is invisible in the words.
constructions.literal_trap: 'de manière à être entendu' read as 'in a manner at being heard'
constructions.example_fr: Parle plus fort, de manière à être entendu du fond.
constructions.example_en: Speak up so that you can be heard at the back.

constructions.schema_form: de peur / crainte que (+ ne) + SUBJONCTIF
constructions.meaning_en: for fear that, lest, so as to avoid X happening
constructions.why_opaque: The clause states what the subject wants to avoid, and it normally carries an expletive 'ne' that is not a negation — so the feared event looks negated when it is not.
constructions.literal_trap: 'de peur qu'on ne l'entende' read as 'for fear that they do not hear him' (exact opposite)
constructions.example_fr: Il chuchotait de peur qu'on ne l'entende.
constructions.example_en: He was whispering so he wouldn't be heard.

constructions.meaning_en: just to, only so as to (informal)
constructions.why_opaque: 'histoire' (story) is emptied of meaning and becomes a downplaying purpose marker equivalent to 'just to'; extremely common in speech and film dialogue.
constructions.literal_trap: 'histoire de dire bonjour' read as 'a story of saying hello'
constructions.example_fr: On est passés, histoire de dire bonjour.
constructions.example_en: We dropped by, just to say hello.

constructions.name_en: de sorte que (so that / with the result that)
constructions.meaning_en: so that (intended) with the subjunctive, or with the result that (actual) with the indicative
constructions.why_opaque: The same three words mean purpose or result depending only on the mood of the following verb, and 'sorte' has nothing to do with kinds or sorting.
constructions.literal_trap: 'de sorte que tout soit prêt' read as 'of the sort that everything is ready'
constructions.example_fr: Range tes affaires de sorte que tout soit prêt demain.
constructions.example_en: Tidy your things away so that everything is ready tomorrow.

constructions.meaning_en: if X (is the case), it's because Y
constructions.why_opaque: 'si' is not hypothetical but presuppositional ('given that'), and the bare 'c'est que' means 'it is because'; the causal link has no word for 'because' anywhere.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Si je te dis ça, c'est que je m'inquiète' read as 'If I tell you that, it is that I'm worried'
constructions.example_fr: Si je te dis ça, c'est que je m'inquiète pour toi.
constructions.example_en: The reason I'm telling you this is that I'm worried about you.

constructions.schema_form: au cas où + CONDITIONNEL (ou seul, en fin de phrase)
constructions.meaning_en: in case, in the event that; used alone at the end of a sentence it means 'just in case'
constructions.why_opaque: 'où' is a place word yet introduces a hypothesis, the verb must be conditional (not subjunctive, unlike most such conjunctions), and the phrase can stand alone with no clause at all.
constructions.literal_trap: 'au cas où il pleuvrait' read as 'at the case where it would rain'
constructions.example_fr: Prends un parapluie, au cas où il pleuvrait.
constructions.example_en: Take an umbrella, in case it rains.

constructions.meaning_en: if only ever so slightly / the slightest bit of X and ...
constructions.why_opaque: 'peu' (little) plus 'pour' produces a threshold condition: the smallest amount is enough for the consequence, an implication no word states.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Pour peu qu'on l'écoute' read as 'for little that one listens to him'
constructions.example_fr: Pour peu qu'on l'écoute, il parle pendant des heures.
constructions.example_en: Give him the slightest encouragement and he'll talk for hours.

constructions.schema_form: à condition que + SUBJONCTIF / à condition de + INFINITIF
constructions.meaning_en: provided that, on condition that
constructions.why_opaque: The conjunction is a frozen prepositional phrase whose complement type flips with the subject: 'que + subjonctif' when the subject changes, 'de + infinitif' when it does not.
constructions.literal_trap: 'à condition que tu viennes' read as 'at condition that you come', or produced with the indicative
constructions.example_fr: Je veux bien t'aider, à condition que tu me préviennes avant.
constructions.example_en: I'm happy to help, provided you let me know in advance.

constructions.schema_form: à moins que (+ ne) + SUBJONCTIF / à moins de + INFINITIF
constructions.meaning_en: unless
constructions.why_opaque: 'moins' (less) builds a negative condition meaning 'unless', and the clause usually contains an expletive 'ne' that does not negate anything — so the exception looks like a negation.
constructions.literal_trap: 'à moins qu'il ne pleuve' read as 'unless it doesn't rain' (the opposite condition)
constructions.example_fr: On part demain, à moins qu'il ne pleuve.
constructions.example_en: We're leaving tomorrow, unless it rains.

constructions.meaning_en: without someone doing something / without it happening
constructions.why_opaque: French subordinates a whole clause under a preposition, which English can only render with 'without' plus a gerund; the clause is subjunctive and often contains a negative-looking word ('personne', 'ne') that is not a second negation.
constructions.literal_trap: 'sans que personne s'en aperçoive' read as 'without that nobody notices' (double negative)
constructions.example_fr: Il est parti sans que personne s'en aperçoive.
constructions.example_en: He left without anyone noticing.

constructions.schema_form: Si + on / tu / vous / nous + IMPARFAIT ?
constructions.meaning_en: how about we ...? / why don't we ...?
constructions.why_opaque: A bare 'if' clause with no main clause and a past-tense verb is a proposal about the future; the sentence looks unfinished and past-referring but is neither.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Si on allait au cinéma ?' read as 'If we went to the cinema...' (an unfinished conditional)
constructions.example_fr: Si on allait au cinéma ce soir ?
constructions.example_en: How about going to the cinema tonight?

constructions.schema_form: ..., sans quoi / faute de quoi + PROPOSITION
constructions.meaning_en: otherwise, failing which, or else
constructions.why_opaque: 'quoi' is a resumptive pronoun standing for the whole preceding clause, producing a sentence connector meaning 'if that does not happen'; the conditional force is entirely structural.
constructions.literal_trap: 'sans quoi l'offre expire' read as 'without what the offer expires'
constructions.example_fr: Signez avant lundi, sans quoi l'offre expire.
constructions.example_en: Sign before Monday, otherwise the offer lapses.

constructions.meaning_en: assuming that / if indeed it is even true that
constructions.why_opaque: Four words with no combinable meaning ('if so much is that') form a sceptical hedge casting doubt on the presupposition, which is pure pragmatics.
constructions.literal_trap: 'si tant est qu'il ait compris' read as 'if so much is that he understood'
constructions.example_fr: Il viendra, si tant est qu'il ait compris la date.
constructions.example_en: He'll come, assuming he even got the date right.

constructions.meaning_en: whose / of which / about which — a relative pronoun that already contains 'de'
constructions.why_opaque: 'dont' silently absorbs the preposition 'de' required by the verb or noun inside the clause, so the English equivalent varies wildly ('that I told you about', 'whose father', 'which I need') and no preposition appears in French.
constructions.literal_trap: Treated as a plain 'that' — 'le film dont je t'ai parlé' read as 'the film that I told you'
constructions.example_fr: Le film dont je t'ai parlé sort demain.
constructions.example_en: The film I told you about comes out tomorrow.

constructions.meaning_en: the thing that ... of / what ... (with a verb built with de)
constructions.why_opaque: 'ce' is an empty placeholder head and 'dont' hides the 'de' that 'avoir besoin de' requires; the English is a single word, 'what'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'ce dont j'avais besoin' read as 'this of which I had need' or 'that which I needed of'
constructions.example_fr: C'est exactement ce dont j'avais besoin.
constructions.example_en: That's exactly what I needed.

constructions.meaning_en: the thing to/about which ... / what ... (with a verb built with à)
constructions.why_opaque: The choice between 'ce que', 'ce dont' and 'ce à quoi' is dictated by the preposition the inner verb takes, information that is invisible in English where all three are 'what'.
constructions.literal_trap: 'ce à quoi je pensais' read as 'this at what I was thinking'
constructions.example_fr: Ce à quoi je pensais, c'est un voyage en train.
constructions.example_en: What I had in mind was a train trip.

constructions.schema_form: NOM + auquel / à laquelle / auxquels / duquel / desquelles + PROPOSITION
constructions.meaning_en: to which / of which / from which
constructions.why_opaque: The preposition is fused into the pronoun and the pronoun agrees in gender and number with a noun that may be several words back, so the learner sees one opaque word where English has two or three.
constructions.literal_trap: 'le problème auquel nous faisons face' read as 'the problem at which we make face'
constructions.example_fr: Le problème auquel nous faisons face est grave.
constructions.example_en: The problem we are facing is a serious one.

constructions.meaning_en: by doing / while doing / on doing — expresses means, simultaneity or condition
constructions.why_opaque: One form covers three unrelated English readings (means, simultaneity, condition) and 'en' never means 'in' here; the subject of the gerund must be the subject of the main verb, which is why 'en tombant' can only refer to the person who got hurt.
constructions.literal_trap: 'Il s'est blessé en tombant' read as 'He hurt himself in falling' with no causal link, or 'while he was falling down'
constructions.example_fr: Il s'est blessé en tombant dans l'escalier.
constructions.example_en: He hurt himself falling down the stairs.
